newsitem.title: USA: DuPont chief sees growth in emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: DuPont chief sees growth in emerging markets.

text.p: DuPont Co. chief executive John Krol said his company will look for business opportunities in "high-growth, emerging markets" around the world where so far it has had little or no presence.

In a news briefing in which he also called for lowering trade barriers and less restrictive government regulation over chemicals, Krol said DuPont's global push would be led by its research strength, joint ventures and acquisitions.
"We intend to be the most successful energy and chemistry-based company in the world," he said. "We will do this by leveraging our global strengths.
In most of Asia, where the company is growing 20 percent a year, DuPont is now seeking a site in China for a nylon venture with BASF AG, Krol said.
Although the company's China sales grew by 40 percent last year, its goal is for only 25 percent in 1997, he said.
"It'll go in fits and starts," he added.

Another area of high-growth potential is eastern Europe, where Dupont saw sales grow by 30 percent last year, albeit to a relatively small $227 million, Krol said. In the former Soviet Union, sales grew by 70 percent last year, he said.
"As eastern European countries move from military-based to market-driven economies, we expect even more opportunity," Krol added.

In western Europe, which accounts for 25 percent of its earnings, DuPont has cut costs and is investing $300-$400 million a year as it seeks to gain market share, offer new applications of products and make aquisitions, he said.

With a South American growth rate of 10 percent a year, the company's sales in that region should reach $2 billion by 2000, he said. In Venezuela, a heavy crude oil joint venture is expected bring in at least 120,000 barrels a day by 2000 and yield DuPont $9 billion over the life of the project, he added.
With about 25 percent of DuPont's U.S. jobs linked directly to exports, Krol called for continued tariff reductions under the World Trade Organization and other regional agreements.

"The region of greatest concern is Asia-Pacific where in some countries we have the right to manufacture there but still don't have the right to sell into that country products we make elsewhere," he said.

Krol supports the North American Free Trade Agreement, which he predicted would extend to the rest of the western hemisphere by 2005, but opposes Washington's unilaterally imposed economic sanctions, which he said would be more effective as multi-lateral efforts with other countries.

He also stressed DuPont's need for protection of intellectual property rights, called for industry involvement in chemical and environmental regulation and called on governments to foster economic growth.
